Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            Before the Court is Defendant Turo, Inc.’s (“Turo”) motion to dismiss. The matter is fully

                                  14   briefed and suitable for decision without oral argument. Accordingly, the hearing set for January

                                  15   8, 2026, was vacated. See Civil L.R. 7-6, Fed. R. Civ. Pro. 78(b). Having read the parties’ papers

                                  16   and carefully considered their arguments and the relevant legal authority, the Court hereby

                                  17   GRANTS Turo’s motion, for the following reasons.

                                  18   I.       BACKGROUND1

                                  19            As described by the company’s declarant, Turo is an online peer-to-peer car sharing

                                  20   platform that connects hosts with guests seeking to book a host’s vehicles. Armstrong Decl. ¶ 3.

                                  21   Turo does not own the vehicles that hosts list for booking on its platform, and it does not maintain

                                  22   the Hosts’ vehicles. Id. ¶ 4.

                                  23            Plaintiff Kriztian Mark Riez alleges that on February 10, 2025, he booked a vehicle listed

                                  24   by a host on Turo’s platform, to be used between February 18 and 20, 2025. See Dkt. 1-1 at 9-10

                                  25

                                  26
                                       1
                                         Though the Court typically accepts the truth of a plaintiff’s allegations for purposes of resolving
                                       a motion to dismiss, given the substance of Turo’s factual attack, the Court considers evidence
                                  27   outside the complaint as well. See Safe Air for Everyone v. Meyer, 373 F.3d 1035, 1039 (9th Cir.
                                       2004) (“In resolving a factual attack on jurisdiction, the district court may review evidence beyond
                                  28   the complaint without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment.”).
                                         Case 3:25-cv-06901-AMO            Document 24         Filed 12/19/25      Page 2 of 5




                                   1   (“car sharing agreement” attached to complaint). Riez asserts the vehicle was contaminated with

                                   2   an undisclosed amount of fentanyl as “confirmed by border authorities.” Compl. at 4. Riez

                                   3   contends that “[o]n or about February 19, 2025, Turo represented to plaintiff that the rental vehicle

                                   4   was safe, clean, and fit for use, in accordance with its advertised standards and Terms of Service.”

                                   5   Compl. at 5. Riez alleges that such representation was false in that “[t]he vehicle was

                                   6   contaminated with fentanyl,” and that Turo had no reasonable ground for believing the

                                   7   representation to be true at the time it made the representation. Id.

                                   8          Riez complains further that, on some unknown date, Turo received a warning, after which

                                   9   it “did nothing . . . just relisted the vehicle, knowingly endangering future renters, families, and

                                  10   children.” Compl. at 4. Riez claims that Turo “denied all responsibility and refused to help,

                                  11   abandoning the plaintiff and a witness to wrongful detainment, PTSD, reputational destruction,

                                  12   and the loss of an $850,000 sponsorship.” Id.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          On July 11, 2025, Riez filed the above-captioned action against Turo in San Francisco

                                  14   Superior Court, alleging claims for (1) general negligence, (2) breach of contract, (3) negligent

                                  15   misrepresentation, (4) concealment, and (5) promissory estoppel. See generally Compl. (Dkt. No.

                                  16   1-1). On July 14, 2025, Turo removed the action to federal court based on diversity jurisdiction.

                                  17   See Dkt. No. 1.

                                  18   II.    DISCUSSION

                                  19          Turo moves to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and failure to state a claim,

                                  20   and it additionally moves to strike Riez’s request for punitive damages. See Dkt. No. 9. The

                                  21   Court takes up the question of subject matter jurisdiction first and, finding such jurisdiction

                                  22   lacking, does not reach the remaining issues.

                                  23          The Court evaluates challenges to Article III standing under Rule 12(b)(1), which governs

                                  24   motions to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Maya v. Centex Corp., 658 F.3d 1060,

                                  25   1067 (9th Cir. 2011). Rule 12(b)(1) motions may be either facial, where the inquiry is confined to

                                  26   the allegations in the complaint, or factual, where the court is permitted to look beyond the

                                  27   complaint to extrinsic evidence. Leite v. Crane Co., 749 F.3d 1117, 1121 (9th Cir. 2014). When a

                                  28   defendant challenges jurisdiction “facially,” all material allegations in the complaint are assumed
                                                                                          2
                                         Case 3:25-cv-06901-AMO            Document 24         Filed 12/19/25      Page 3 of 5




                                   1   true, and the court determines whether the factual allegations are sufficient to invoke the court’s

                                   2   subject matter jurisdiction. Id. When a defendant makes a factual challenge “by presenting

                                   3   affidavits or other evidence properly brought before the court, the party opposing the motion must

                                   4   furnish affidavits or other evidence necessary to satisfy its burden of establishing subject matter

                                   5   jurisdiction.” Safe Air for Everyone v. Meyer, 373 F.3d 1035, 1039 (9th Cir. 2004); see also Leite,

                                   6   749 F.3d at 1121. The court need not presume the truthfulness of the plaintiff’s allegations under

                                   7   a factual attack. Wood v. City of San Diego, 678 F.3d 1075, 1083 n.8 (9th Cir. 2012).

                                   8          “Article III confines the federal judicial power to the resolution of ‘Cases’ and

                                   9   ‘Controversies.’ For there to be a case or controversy under Article III, the plaintiff must have a

                                  10   ‘personal stake’ in the case – in other words, standing.” TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S.

                                  11   413, 423 (2021) (citation omitted). To establish standing, “(1) the plaintiff [must have] suffered

                                  12   an injury in fact, i.e., one that is sufficiently ‘concrete and particularized’ and ‘actual or imminent,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   not conjectural or hypothetical,’ (2) the injury is ‘fairly traceable’ to the challenged conduct, and

                                  14   (3) the injury is ‘likely’ to be ‘redressed by a favorable decision.’ ” Bates v. United Parcel Serv.,

                                  15   Inc., 511 F.3d 974, 985 (9th Cir. 2007) (quoting Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555,

                                  16   560-61 (1992)). “To establish an injury in fact, a plaintiff must show that he or she suffered ‘an

                                  17   invasion of a legally protected interest’ that is ‘concrete and particularized.’ ” In re Facebook,

                                  18   Inc. Internet Tracking Litig., 956 F.3d 589, 597 (9th Cir. 2020) (quoting Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins,

                                  19   578 U.S. 330, 339 (2016), as revised (May 24, 2016)).

                                  20          Here, Riez alleges that as a result of Turo’s alleged actions, he suffered (1) wage loss,

                                  21   (2) hospital and medical expenses, (3) general damage, (4) loss of earning capacity, (5) emotional

                                  22   distress, (6) reputational harm, (7) punitive damages, and (8) legal expenses. See Compl. at 3.

                                  23   Riez seeks compensatory damages, punitive damages, and damages in the amount of

                                  24   $1,500,000.00. Id. These vague purported harms are not supported by factual allegations and fail

                                  25   on multiple grounds. First, Riez does not claim that he or anyone else suffered any physical harm

                                  26   from fentanyl exposure. Second, he does not identify when he ever informed Turo about the

                                  27   alleged fentanyl exposure, despite asserting that Turo refused to help him. Third, Riez does not

                                  28   specify the nature of his “$850,000 sponsorship” or how the presence of fentanyl in the vehicle
                                                                                          3
                                         Case 3:25-cv-06901-AMO             Document 24         Filed 12/19/25     Page 4 of 5




                                   1   caused him to lose it. Fourth, Riez does not specify how this incident caused him reputational

                                   2   harm, particularly given that Riez does not establish that “border authorities” took any action

                                   3   against him. Finally, he does not acknowledge or engage with the Terms of Service he agreed to

                                   4   before this booking occurred.

                                   5           More importantly, Riez’s injuries are not traceable to Turo’s challenged action because

                                   6   Riez does not allege that Turo took any action contributing to his injuries. All Turo did, according

                                   7   to the complaint, was allow Riez, as the guest, to book a non-party host’s vehicle over Turo’s

                                   8   online platform. For example, Riez does not allege Turo contaminated the vehicle with fentanyl

                                   9   or that Turo knew the vehicle was contaminated prior to his injury because Turo does not possess,

                                  10   clean, or otherwise physically inspect any of the vehicles listed on its online platform. Armstrong

                                  11   Decl. ¶ 4. It is the host’s responsibility to “to ensure their vehicles are in safe and operable

                                  12   condition.” Ex. A at 17. As the operator of a peer-to-peer marketplace, Turo connects hosts and
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   guests with one another and establishes certain rules around issues like vehicle safety and

                                  14   cleanliness. Armstrong Decl. ¶ 4. The vehicle was owned, controlled, and operated by another

                                  15   Turo user, a non-party host. Id. ¶ 4. To the extent Riez suffered a legally cognizable injury, he

                                  16   has not alleged facts connecting Turo’s conduct to that injury.

                                  17           Further, to the extent Riez alleges Turo allowed the vehicle to be relisted on its platform

                                  18   after the vaguely-described incident, Riez fails to allege how he was injured by such relisting.

                                  19   Compl. at 6, FR-6 (alleging that Turo “put the public at risk”). Plaintiff does not have a concrete

                                  20   or particular injury to assert a claim on this basis.

                                  21           Because Turo did not contribute to Riez’s alleged injuries after being stopped at the border,

                                  22   his injury is not sufficiently traceable to Turo’s challenged action for Riez to establish Article III

                                  23   standing. Riez fails to meet his burden establishing Article III standing because none of his

                                  24   purported injuries are traceable to Turo’s conduct.

                                  25   III.    CONCLUSION

                                  26           Because Riez fails to offer facts establishing injury in fact, and because Riez fails to

                                  27   establish that any injury is traceable to Turo’s conduct, Riez lacks Article III standing to bring this

                                  28
                                                                                           4
                                         Case 3:25-cv-06901-AMO           Document 24         Filed 12/19/25      Page 5 of 5




                                   1   action against Turo. The Court therefore GRANTS Turo’s motion to dismiss for lack of subject

                                   2   matter jurisdiction. The Court DISMISSES the complaint with leave to amend.

                                   3          Riez may file an amended complaint by no later than January 16, 2026. No additional

                                   4   parties or claims may be added without leave of Court or stipulation of Turo. Though the Court

                                   5   did not address in this order Turo’s additional attacks on the complaint, including a motion to

                                   6   dismiss for failure to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6) and a motion to strike the claim for

                                   7   punitive damages under Rule 12(f), the Court cautions Riez to consider those arguments in

                                   8   preparing an amended complaint.

                                   9          Riez is advised that there is helpful information for self-represented litigants at

                                  10   http://cand.uscourts.gov/proselitigants, including the Northern District’s Representing Yourself in

                                  11   Federal Court: A Handbook for Pro Se Litigants. Riez is also encouraged to seek the assistance

                                  12   of the free Legal Help Center operated by the Bar Association of San Francisco. A litigant may
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   schedule an appointment by signing up in the appointment book located on the table outside the

                                  14   door of the Center or by calling the Legal Help Center appointment line at 415-782-8982.

                                  15

                                  16          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                  17   Dated: December 16, 2025

                                  18
                                  19
                                                                                                     ARACELI MARTÍNEZ-OLGUÍN
                                  20                                                                 United States District Judge
